value.overview: The Ivory-billed Woodcreeper (Xiphorhynchus flavigaster) is a medium-sized woodcreeper of Mexico and northern Central America. It is named for its long, pale, slightly curved bill and is usually found in dry or moist woodland, forest edges, and second growth. This largely resident bird climbs trunks and large branches while searching for animal prey beneath bark and among vines. In Costa Rica, it reaches the northwestern part of its range and is associated mainly with Pacific-slope habitats.
value.classification: The Ivory-billed Woodcreeper belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae. It is one of several closely related Xiphorhynchus woodcreepers found in the Neotropics.
value.identification: It is about 20–25 cm long, with a long, fairly heavy, slightly decurved bill that is pale ivory or horn-colored. The upperparts are brown to grayish olive with buff streaks, while the throat, breast, and belly are buffy or ochraceous with dark streaking. The wings and tail are usually rich chestnut, creating a noticeable contrast with the back. A pale eyebrow and streaked face are useful field marks. Sexes are similar.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from western, southern, and eastern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a localized resident at the northern Pacific end of the country, especially on the Pacific slope and in the Nicoya Peninsula region; it is not widespread across the Caribbean lowlands or most of central and southern Costa Rica. It uses tropical deciduous and semideciduous woodland, moist forest, forest edge, secondary growth, and sometimes pine-oak or other mixed woodland, from lowlands into foothills.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and nonmigratory throughout its range. In Costa Rica, birds are expected to occur year-round in suitable northwestern Pacific habitats rather than arriving as seasonal migrants, although local movements may follow food availability or changing habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The Ivory-billed Woodcreeper nests in cavities, including natural holes and abandoned cavities made by other birds, usually in trees or large branches. The breeding biology is not fully documented across all parts of its range, but the species is believed to form pairs and defend breeding territories. A small clutch, commonly around two eggs, is typical of related woodcreepers. In Costa Rica, breeding activity is most likely during the local dry-to-early-wet-season period, but detailed dates and nest records are limited.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of arthropods and other invertebrates, including insects, spiders, and larvae, with occasional small vertebrate prey reported. It usually forages alone or in pairs, hitching upward along trunks and branches and probing bark, crevices, dead leaf clusters, and vine tangles with its long bill. It may also join mixed-species feeding flocks, especially where woodland structure provides abundant mature trees and rough bark.
value.behavior: This is a diurnal, trunk-climbing bird that typically moves upward in short hops, bracing itself with its stiff tail and strong feet. It may spiral around trunks or work along the undersides of large limbs. The Ivory-billed Woodcreeper is often inconspicuous because it stays within vegetation, but its calls and repeated movement on tree trunks can reveal its presence. It sometimes forages at forest edges and in older secondary growth, not only in undisturbed forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not considered to indicate a major global decline, although local populations may be affected by habitat loss and changes in woodland quality.
